SUBJECT:  GENERAL PLAN UPDATE – POLICY FRAMEWORKS

ISSUE
Should the City Council receive a presentation on the General Plan Update (Palmdale
2045) status and provide feedback on the draft policy frameworks.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Receive an update on the General Plan Update (Palmdale 2045); and
  2. Provide feedback on the draft policy frameworks.

BACKGROUND
Palmdale 2045 is a four-year project that commenced in January 2019 when the City
Council approved a professional services agreement with the City’s preferred consultant,
Raimi + Associates. The General Plan serves as the City’s primary guide for land use and
development decisions and is a key tool for influencing and improving the quality of life
for residents and businesses. As such, it serves as the “blueprint” for future development
and conservation of a community. The General Plan will help the City plan for important
community issues such as new growth, housing needs and environmental protection. It
also sets the stage for future social, physical, and economic development of the City. It
addresses issues that impact the entire City, such as how land is used, where buildings
are constructed, and priority areas for future parks.

DISCUSSION
Following the approval of the preferred land use alternative in March 2021, the General
Plan Team (GP Team) crafted policy frameworks, which are an interim step to preparing
the Draft General Plan Elements and include proposed goals and policies. Between June
and August, the GP Team hosted six joint General Plan Advisory Committee (GPAC)
meetings and public workshops to solicit feedback from the community on the proposed
goals and policies as outlined within TABLE 1.

Policy Frameworks Reports

Each policy framework covers one topic to be included in the General Plan and lays out
initial policy concepts for community review and reaction. The reports are separated into
major sections; introduction, where we are now, what we heard about this topic, where
we want to be in the future, future outcomes, and draft goals and policies. The draft goals
and policies reflect feedback from the community, GPAC, Planning Commission, City
Council, and include some of the applicable goals and policies carried over from the 1993
Palmdale General Plan.

Outreach

The joint policy frameworks meetings were advertised through a comprehensive and
ongoing digital and print marketing strategy which included the following activities:

    Digital press releases in the Antelope Valley Press, Antelope Valley Times, and
  the Antelope Valley Daily News
    The Palmdale Minute weekly video segment
    Project database e-blasts in English and Spanish
    Posting on the City’s social media platforms in English and Spanish
    Council announcements
    Automall billboard
    Workshop flyers were distributed to the following organizations and locations:
  o City Hall
  o SAVES
    Print advertisements were placed in Palmdale Connections Magazine

Community Feedback on the Policy Frameworks

The policy frameworks were presented virtually to the community through an overview
presentation by a GP Team topic expert and using a web-based program, called Konveio,
that allows the viewers to read the document, post comments, and review and react to
comments posted by other community members.

Each policy framework meeting included small group discussions with specific prompts
related to the proposed goals and policies and an opportunity for public comment. Policy
documents were provided to GPAC members prior to each meeting. In addition, all policy
framework documents were posted on the Palmdale 2045 website with additional
background information.

Attached for reference are General Plan policy frameworks (ATTACHMENTS 1-8) and
joint GPAC and Public Workshop meeting minutes (ATTACHMENTS 9-13).

As indicated within TABLE 1, one of the GPAC meetings (health/environmental
justice/equity/parks/public facilities) occurred after preparation of this staff report. As
such, draft minutes for the meeting will be provided as soon as they are available. In
addition, policy frameworks for noise, air quality, conservation, open space, and cultural
resources are being prepared and are anticipated to be available for review and comment
by the public in September.

FISCAL IMPACT
Long term fiscal impacts will vary depending on the final goals, policies, and
implementing actions within the adopted General Plan.

   Sustainability, Climate Action, and Resilience Policy Framework | Spring 2021

Sustainability, Climate
Action, and Resilience
Policy Framework
Introduction
The City of Palmdale has embarked on a comprehensive update to its General Plan, called
“Envision Palmdale 2045: A Complete Community,” to create a forward-looking document that will
serve as the blueprint for the City’s vision through the year 2045. The goals, policies, and actions in
Palmdale 2045 will serve as a compass for decision-makers and will shape future plans and actions
of the City. This revised policy document will replace the 1993 General Plan.

This sustainability, climate, and resilience policy framework is an interim step in the General Plan
Update process prior to drafting the elements (or chapters). This framework highlights key
outcomes and performance metrics related to sustainability and includes a draft policy framework
that includes goals, policies, and implementation activities. This policy framework was developed
by compiling feedback from community members, General Plan Advisory Committee members,
Planning Commission, and City Council. This framework synthesizes critical issues and policy
approaches by describing key strengths and opportunities, challenges, and threats, and what we
heard from the community.

What is Sustainability?
Sustainability is often defined as the ability to meet the needs of the current generation without
compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs. Sustainability is a cross-cutting
issue that centers on environmental, social equity, and economic considerations. In specific terms,
taking a sustainability approach means conserving energy and water, diverting waste from
landfills, preparing for the potential impacts of climate change, and reducing greenhouse gas
emissions, among others.

The importance of practicing sustainability is becoming a greater priority due to the potential
impacts of climate change. Climate is the long-term behavior of the atmosphere – typically

  City of Palmdale General Plan Update | 1
   Sustainability, Climate Action, and Resilience Policy Framework | Spring 2021

represented as averages – for a given time of year. This includes average annual temperature,
snowpack, or rainfall. Human emissions of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases are
important drivers of global climate change. Greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere,
resulting in warming over time. This atmospheric warming leads to other changes in earth systems,
including changing patterns of rainfall and snow, melting of glaciers and ice, and warming and the
changing chemistry of oceans.

California, the Antelope Valley, and the City of Palmdale are already experiencing the effects of a
changing climate. Both gradual climate change (e.g., wildfire risk) and climate hazard events (e.g.,
extreme heat days or weather events) expose people, infrastructure, buildings and properties, and
ecosystems to a wide range of stress-inducing and hazardous situations. These hazards and their
impacts often have a disproportionate effect on the most sensitive populations in the City.

The impacts of climate change in the future depends in part on the amount of greenhouse gas
emissions that are present in the atmosphere now and in the future. Greenhouse gas emissions
are driven by economic systems, land use patterns, transportation and energy systems, resource
use, and other social and political factors. By reducing greenhouse emissions, the City can help to
mitigate the long-term impacts of climate change. Adaptation strategies such as increasing shade
and increasing light-colored surfaces can reduce the negative effects of high heat days. Combining
climate strategies with other efforts related to water conservation, energy efficiency, recycling, and
ecosystem protection helps to increase the overall sustainability and livability of the community.

Where We Are Now
To date, the City has few key plans in place with the direct purpose of reducing greenhouse gas
emissions citywide. The City has been implementing its 2011 Palmdale Energy Action Plan (PEAP).
Efforts include implementing interior and exterior lighting and HVAC upgrades across City facilities
and installing solar panels to generate renewable and carbon-free energy. The City has also
installed 21 publicly accessible electric vehicle (EV) chargers, including five DC Fast Chargers to
support the transition to EVs. Most importantly, the City is moving forward with a community
choice aggregation program (CCA) to supply local carbon-free electricity to residents and
businesses starting in October of 2022. Focusing on community emission mitigation provides the
City with the greatest opportunity to reduce emissions and realize sustainability co-benefits of
climate action measures.

The City’s most recent greenhouse gas (GHG) inventory for calendar year 2017 estimates total
community emissions of 1,005,891 Tonnes of Carbon Dioxide equivalent (MTCO2e). Transportation
related emissions are the largest contributor to community emissions, accounting for 59%,
followed by residential energy use, accounting for 20%, and nonresidential energy use, accounting

for 15% of emissions. However, nonresidential energy use data is incomplete because of privacy
and aggregation laws, it is likely higher, which would increase total emissions. The remaining 6% of
emissions are made up of solid waste, off-road equipment, water and wastewater, and industrial
sources (see Figure 1).

Since transportation is the largest contributor to GHG emissions, the inventory suggests the need
to pursue sustainable land use patterns of development, transportation-oriented development,
public transit improvements, active transportation network enhancements, create programs to
reduce vehicle use for short trips, and to better match Palmdale residents with employers to
reduce vehicle miles traveled (VMT). Implementation of GHG reduction measures provides the City
with the opportunity to realize co-benefits. For example, VMT reduction reduces GHG emissions,
but also helps to improve air quality, lessen traffic and congestion, and create safer roadways for
pedestrians and cyclists.

Furthermore, despite projected growth in population and jobs with the General Plan Update
Preferred Land Use Alternative, the adjusted business-as-usual (ABAU) forecast projects that
emissions are expected to fall from 919,905 MTCO2e in baseline year 2005 to 803,309 MTCO2e in
2045, a 13% decrease. This forecast illustrates the importance of supporting the State’s climate
targets to reduce emissions statewide and kickstart local actions.

Resilience issues facing the City include increases in high heat days from 11 in 2017 to 17 in 2045
according to Cal-Adapt. Wildfires in the Angeles National Forest and other nearby forested and
natural areas and the associated property damage and worsened air quality from wildfires are also

  City of Palmdale General Plan Update | 3

a concern. Other issues are related to potable water supply and impacts from climate-related
persistent drought conditions. Land use modifications, water efficiency and stormwater
management, renewable energy generation and storage, and increased organic waste diversion
are all adaptive approaches that can improve sustainability on an ongoing basis while also
increasing resilience to both the stressors and shocks related to climate change. The City is located
close to the San Andreas fault and other seismically active areas. The Local Hazard Mitigation Plan
(LHMP) provides guidance for preparing for and responding to earthquakes and other disasters.
Many of the measures established in the LHMP can also be activated to respond to climate-related
events such as high heat, poor air quality, extreme storm, events, or temporary disruption of
electricity service.

In addition to climate concerns, sustainability issues to be addressed in the General Plan update
include water quality and supply, waste management, ecosystem stewardship, increasing
environmental literacy, providing equitable access to open spaces, and supporting the health,
well-being, and spirit of the community.

Introduction
The City of Palmdale has embarked on a comprehensive update to its General Plan, called
“Envision Palmdale 2045: A Complete Community,” to create a forward-looking document that will
serve as the blueprint for the City’s vision through the year 2045. The goals, policies, and actions in
the 2045 General Plan will serve as a compass for decision-makers and will shape future City plans
and actions. This revised document will replace the 1993 General Plan.

This land use and urban design policy framework is an interim step in the General Plan Update
process prior to drafting the elements. This framework highlights key outcomes and performance
metrics and includes a draft policy framework that includes goals, policies, and implementation
activities. This policy framework was developed by compiling feedback from community members,
General Plan Advisory Committee members, Planning Commission, and City Council. This
framework synthesizes critical issues and policy approaches by describing key strengths and
opportunities, challenges, and threats.

Where We Are Now
The following section highlights strengths, opportunities, challenges, and threats that have been
identified by the planning team throughout the course of the General Plan update process, as well
as input heard from community members, that have shaped the Land Use policy framework.

  •  Strengths. The natural environment is one of the most defining characteristics of
  Palmdale. Community members exude pride and appreciation for the open space and
  mountain views in Palmdale, expressing the desire for continued preservation through the
  General Plan Update. Many community members speak to the small-town atmosphere in
  Palmdale, which is unique for a community of over 150,000 people. Palmdale’s
  comparatively affordable housing allows residents a chance for homeownership. In
  addition to Palmdale’s physical characteristics, it is home to some of the most innovative

  City of Palmdale General Plan Update | 1
   Land Use, Community Design and Housing Policy Framework | Spring 2021

  research and development in the Aerospace industry with Air Force Plant 42, which
  supplies high quality STEM jobs for the region.
  •  Opportunities. Palmdale is experiencing a unique point in its history; several long-range
  major transportation improvements are planned, which will make travel to Palmdale faster
  and more efficient. This provides the opportunity for new jobs, housing, and regular
  visitors to Palmdale. The City has begun leveraging these improvements through the
  planned development of downtown Palmdale. These improvements coupled with the
  City’s proximity to both the Los Angeles basin and the High Desert provide tremendous
  opportunities for an infusion into the local economy.
  •  Challenges. While Palmdale has many strengths and opportunities, challenges exist
  related to the sheer expanse of land within City limits. Large swaths of the City do not have
  existing infrastructure leading to development constraints. Isolated suburban
  communities and topography have led to a discontinuous circulation pattern that creates
  challenges for pedestrians and non-motorized forms of travel. Single-family housing is
  abundant, but other housing types are lacking due to limiting development regulations.
  Palmdale residents identified an ongoing division between East and West Palmdale and
  competition for services and amenities. Another challenge is the mismatch between
  available jobs and residents’, leading to a daily exodus down to the Los Angeles basin for
  work.
  •  Threats. While Palmdale’s geographic location provides ample opportunities, it also
  comes with inherent threats. Local wildland fire and geologic hazards threaten existing and
  future development in Palmdale. Noise and hazardous materials from existing businesses
  have the potential to threaten quality of life, and water scarcity threatens future
  development in Palmdale.

  o Rationale: Continued economic vitality is tied to the success of Palmdale’s

  attract skilled employment and the associated fiscal benefits.

  o Rationale: The City currently has a low amount of office land use, and these uses
  are predicted to have strong market demand (medical office, remote work,

  o Rationale: Taking advantage of new transit investments will mean locating a

  o  Require new homes to provide a primary entryway and windows facing the street.
  o  Strongly encourage new subdivisions and master planned projects to include a
  diversity of housing types and architecture styles, where possible.

  City of Palmdale General Plan Update | 10
   Land Use, Community Design and Housing Policy Framework | Spring 2021

  o  For construction of new small-scale housing and minor subdivision projects, design
  site plans that provide amenities and integrated networks for walking and
  bicycling.

Key Districts and Centers

  •  Goal 8: Growth of a transit-oriented community near high-speed rail that combines
  high-quality mixed-use development, a Downtown ‘feel,’ office employment,
  affordable housing, and improved walkability/bikeability.
  o  Develop community gathering spaces, including plazas and pocket parks, near the
  future multimodal transit station.
  o  Reinforce Avenue Q with development patterns that support the future multimodal
  station in a sustainable approach that creates a well-connected mobility network
  around the area improved by the Complete Streets Project.
  o  Design the buildings facing Avenue Q to reflect the vision for a new "main street" –
  active uses, street-oriented entrances, tall floor-to-ceiling heights, reduced
  setbacks (unless adjacent to a plaza or park).

   Land Use, Community Design and Housing Policy Framework | Spring 2021

  o  Evolve the existing Palmdale Transportation Center into an attractive and unique
  multimodal transit gateway.
  o  Require minimum development densities/intensities in certain areas such as the
  Palmdale Transit Area Specific Plan (PTASP) area to promote sufficient
  development that allows active placemaking.
  o  Enhance transit and pedestrian linkages to surrounding areas to create a multi-
  modal transit and pedestrian-oriented center.
  o  Implement urban design guidelines and features that encourage pedestrian
  activity and reduce automobile use.
  o  Establish the future multimodal high speed rail station area as a regional and local
  destination by developing mixed-use retail, residential and office buildings..
  o  Continue to provide assistance to support small locally-owned businesses and
  develop a mechanism to support building upkeep and maintenance, signage, and
  façade improvements for businesses in the PTASP area.

  o  Seek to attract a new major higher education institution.
  o  Encourage the formation of two education districts:
    Near Antelope Valley Community College and Palmdale High School

    In the vacant area on the northern side of Palmdale Boulevard and 47th

  o  Allow and encourage supportive retail, offices, and housing.

•  Goal 10: Employment growth through expanded operations onsite and by preserving
  the buffer between Plant 42 and the rest of the City.
  o  Support continued growth of Plant 42 operations in the Aerospace Industrial land
  use district. Maintain sufficient land to accommodate a wide variety of industrial
  uses to meet military and community needs.
  o  Continue to buffer this area from adjacent, non-compatible residential and
  commercial uses.
  o  Limit non-industrial uses from locating in the Airport Industrial area (aside from
  uses that directly support Plant 42 or airport operations).
  o  Avoid residential uses greater than one dwelling unit per acre in the Accident
  Prevention Zones (APZs).
  o  Maintain vehicular infrastructure and improve circulation to accommodate the
  unique demands for aerospace workplaces.

  compatibility with adjacent non-industrial uses.
  o  Minimize land use compatibility conflicts that discourage attraction and retention
  of production, distribution, and service and repair businesses in areas zoned for
  industrial use.
  o  Encourage master planning and infrastructure funding districts within industrial
  areas to ensure adequate and comprehensive provision of infrastructure and
  efficient, attractive designs, through cohesive planning of larger development
  projects.
  o  Adopt development standards for industrial uses near residential uses, to ensure
  compatibility and aesthetically pleasing views from adjacent rights­ of-way,
  including but not limited to standards for screening of outdoor storage, locations
  of loading and refuse disposal areas, height, bulk, impervious surface area,
  architectural enhancement, landscaping, and other measures as deemed
  appropriate.

  regulation and supportive policies/actions.
  o  Establish flexible development standards in the Employment Flex designation that
  allow industrial uses to make building improvements and change with market
  conditions.
  o  Expand a core area of light industrial and service uses that provide middle-income
  jobs for Palmdale residents.
  o  Buffer heavy industrial uses and light industrial uses, such as general services, light
  manufacturing, and storage uses from residential neighborhoods.
  o  Adjust zoning and parking requirements as necessary to ensure reinvestment can
  occur in buildings while maintaining industrial uses.
  o  Incentivize growth of office and commercial spaces suitable and affordable for
  local businesses through development requirements and community benefits.
  o  Allow lot assembly to allow businesses to grow and expand.

  o  Allow and encourage a mix of public and private medical, health, and wellness uses
  including emergency medical facilities, medical and supportive offices, healthcare
  clinics and pharmacies in this designation.
  o  Expand upon the existing Palmdale Regional Medical Center (Palmdale Boulevard
  and 10th Street West)
  o  Create two new health and wellness districts:
    Along Palmdale Boulevard and 40th/45th Streets
    Adjacent to Kaiser Permanente (East Avenue S and 45th Street East)

  o  Support a network of vibrant mixed-use activity centers located throughout the
  City’s residential areas to create 20-minute “complete” neighborhoods.
  o  Provide a mix of residential uses and daily goods and services within the Village
  Centers in a mixed-use setting.
  o  Implement new mixed-use land use designations to support Village Centers.
  o  Consider design strategies that enhance unique identity for each of the Village
  Centers.
  o  Introduce new public gathering places in Village Centers such as publicly accessible
  plazas or courtyards.
  o  Create appropriate transitions to existing residential neighborhoods by placing
  two-to-three story residential over ground floor retail/services towards arterial
  streets and alley-loaded townhouses abutting existing residences.
  o  Improve walk, bike, and transit access to Village Centers, by connecting to the
  larger pedestrian and bicycle networks.

  •  Goal 15: Allow for a gradual mixed-use evolution at Antelope Valley Mall from a single-
  use center into a mixed-use community gathering place.
  o  Allow a broad range of low/medium-density residential and commercial uses at the
  Antelope Valley Mall.
  o  Work with developers to effectuate redevelopment of big-box retail with higher-
  density developments such as vertical or horizontal mixed use.
  o  Allow a diverse range of retail establishments of any size provided they comply
  with frontage design requirements.
  •  Goal 16: Mineral resource extraction contained to its present location and maintain
  compatibility with neighboring residential uses.
  o  Avoid import of raw materials. Processing of on-site materials should be the
  primary use.
  o  Ancillary uses allowed on the site should be only those uses normally associated
  with extraction and/or processing of on-site materials.
  o  Ensure that measures to control noise, dust and erosion/sedimentation are applied
  to on-going mining activities.
  o  To the extent feasible, require screening of equipment, stockpiles or wastepiles
  from public view.
  o  Evaluate truck access to and from the site in order to reduce impacts generated by
  truck traffic, such as road deterioration, noise and safety concerns, which affect
  nearby residents.

New Residential Neighborhoods
Figure 13: Areas designated as Specific Plan

  •  Goal 17: Modified and existing Specific Plans strive to relate to and integrate with
  adjacent existing and future land uses.
  o  When modifications to a Specific Plan are proposed, require the following:
    Provide connections to regional trails and natural open spaces for all
  residential units.
    Protections for Joshua Trees and other critical desert species.
    Review compliance with Hillside Ordinance for viewshed protection.
  o  Ensure the creation of new Village Centers organized around a central focal point
  such as a park, school, civic building, or neighborhood retail as development
  occurs in Specific Plan areas, including:
    Anaverde Nuevo/City Ranch Specific Plan
    Ritter Ranch Specific Plan
    Lockheed Specific Plan
  o  Encourage the creation of new Village Centers in Planned Development (PD) areas,
  including:

  City of Palmdale General Plan Update | 20
   Land Use, Community Design and Housing Policy Framework | Spring 2021

    Quail Valley PD
    Joshua Ranch PD
    Aero PD
    The Strata PD
•  Goal 18: New Specific Plans are implemented through development of new
  neighborhoods that are connected, sustainable, diverse, and clustered.
  o  Require development of commercial uses and amenities during key phases of
  buildout of residential portions of a Specific Plan.
  o  Require rural neighborhoods and clustered development in steeper and
  topographically constrained areas and use these development types to preserve
  the significant natural amenities.
  o  Avoid grading or siting of dwelling units on the north facing side of Ritter Ridge or
  other major ridgelines.
  o  Strive to create an undeveloped or rural greenbelt around the City comprised of
  natural areas, parks and open space, and agricultural/utility lands.
•  Goal 19: All new major development in the City is designed to support high-quality
  neighborhoods.
  o  Require new development provide multiple amenities, a beautiful public realm,
  and be consistent with the City’s vision for complete neighborhoods.
  o  Require new developments to be designed for and provided with adequate public
  services and infrastructure. Require that these public facilities and services be
  provided concurrently with development to ensure a high quality of life for
  residents.
  o  Strive for a high level of connectivity of residents to neighborhood services through
  site design, open space linkages, and bicycle facilities. Plan for 90 percent of
  residents (except for rural residential) to be within a half-mile walking distance of
  retail and neighborhood services.
  o  Provide new trails systems that connect to the regional system.
  o  Provide a diversity of architectural styles.
  o  To the greatest extent feasible, preserve the natural topographic features during
  the planning and development process. Utilize physical advantages of the site to
  minimize visual impacts.
  o  Require clustered single family and multifamily development in less constrained
  areas, transferring density from areas constrained by seismic, drainage, rights-of-
  way, or other conditions based on technical studies.

  City of Palmdale General Plan Update | 21
   Land Use, Community Design and Housing Policy Framework | Spring 2021

Existing Neighborhood Improvements
  •  Goal 20: Neighborhoods with a range of housing opportunities that allow people of all
  ages, abilities, socio-economic status, and family sizes to live in Palmdale.
  o  Promote residential infill development, where appropriate, as indicated by the new
  Mixed Neighborhoods land use designations (MN-1, MN-2, MN-3, MN-4)
  o  Maximize opportunities for residential development through infill and
  redevelopment of vacant parcels by facilitating parcel aggregation and
  streamlining permit processing for infill applications.
  o  Permit a range of residential densities and housing types throughout the City,
  rather than concentrating higher densities in limited areas.
  o  Direct the location of senior and multi-family housing to areas accessible to public
  transportation, supportive commercial uses, and community facilities.
  o  Encourage and allow a variety of housing types developed at a range of densities to
  serve varying household types, including, but not limited to, single-family attached
  and detached, accessory dwelling units, multi-family apartments, townhomes,
  duplexes, triplexes, quadplexes, and condominiums.
  o  Facilitate housing for seniors, special needs groups, including the developmentally
  disabled, and non-traditional family groups by allowing a diverse range of housing
  configurations that are Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) compliant & flexible.
  o  Promote development of housing types that support multi-generational
  households and opportunities to age in place.
  Figure 14: Areas designated as Single-Family Residential and Neighborhood Residential

  City of Palmdale General Plan Update | 22
   Land Use, Community Design and Housing Policy Framework | Spring 2021

•  Goal 21: Improved walkability and connectivity in existing neighborhoods, through
  increased permeability and access through large blocks.
  o  Provide pedestrian/bicycle connections to trails and open space where
  appropriate and where indicated in past planning efforts.
  o  According to the General Plan street hierarchy, require key boulevards and
  neighborhood connectors to be (re)designed, constructed and operated as
  multimodal boulevards, not wide, high-speed streets.
  o  Introduce new trails systems that connect to the regional system.
  o  Work towards a goal of having 90 percent of residents living within quarter-mile
  walking distances of a dedicated park, school, or multi-use trail.
•  Goal 22: Maintain the character of rural areas.
  o  Avoid designating land for higher density uses where prevailing existing
  development patterns are rural residential with lot sizes of one acre or more.
  o  Ensure that development within the area generally located south of West Avenue S
  and west of Sierra Highway is compatible with and complimentary to existing
  development by requiring that future subdivisions provide large residential lots
  and that future commercial development not extend further west than the City
  park and ride facility located on Geiger Avenue.
  o  Permit neighborhood commercial development within rural areas to serve the
  needs of these areas, provided that such projects provide safe, logical, and
  functional access for pedestrian and equestrian users from the adjacent
  neighborhoods.
  o  Improve the condition of unpaved streets in rural areas.
  o  Enforce County standards and requirements regarding septic systems.
  o  Require that development near the intersection of Avenue S and State Route 14 is
  complimentary to lake, surrounding hillside, and mountain views by minimizing
  building heights and viewshed impacts; and is consistent with sound water quality
  management practices by providing a minimum 100-foot setback from the
  historical high-water mark of Lake Palmdale and meeting other relevant
  environmental standards.
  o  Provide a 1,000-foot buffer between Antelope Valley Landfill operations and
  residential developments.
  o  Consider annexation as a logical extension of the City boundaries as neighboring
  properties are annexed and adjacent properties are developed.
  o  Before initiating annexation, evaluate the fiscal, infrastructural and land use
  impacts of proposed annexations to the City, as well as the desires of inhabitants
  within these areas.

Housing Goals and Policies
  •  Goal 23: Promote the construction of a variety of residential development
  opportunities for all income groups.
  o  Encourage the production of housing for all segments of the City’s population,
  including all income levels and those with special needs.
  o  Encourage a variety of housing types such as a single-family attached
  (townhomes), multifamily units, planned unit developments, mixed-use housing,
  and other housing types to fulfill regional housing needs.
  o  Encourage the development of new affordable units through the provision of
  incentives.
  o  Encourage the development of housing that is affordable to lower income groups
  in areas well served by public transportation, schools, retail, and other services.
  •  Goal 24: Preserve and improve the existing supply of affordable housing.
  o  Require that all units developed under any of the City affordable housing programs
  remain affordable for the longest possible time or at least 30 years.
  o  Use regulatory and financial tools to make mobile home spaces permanently
  affordable.
  o  Preserve or replace units with expiring subsidies.
  •  Goal 25: Mitigate local government constraints on housing.
  o  Assess financial impacts of zone changes on housing affordability.
  o  Assess feasibility of land use concessions and fee reductions to make new housing
  more affordable.
  o  Revise the Zoning Ordinance when necessary to remove constraints in compliance
  with State law.
  •  Goal 26: Promote equal housing for all persons regardless of their special
  characteristics as protected under State and Federal fair housing laws.
  o  Ensure that mixed income housing is focused in areas that have access to transit
  and resources, specifically in Residential Neighborhoods of RN2 and above and all
  the Mixed-Use Districts.
  o  Provide fair housing services that include public information, counseling, and
  investigation.
  •  Goal 27: Facilitate adequate housing for households with special needs.
  o  Permit a variety of housing types for seniors including dependent housing units
  and congregate housing with supportive services.

  City of Palmdale General Plan Update | 25
   Land Use, Community Design and Housing Policy Framework | Spring 2021

  o  Recognize the unique characteristics of elderly and disabled households and
  address the special needs of these households.
  o  Establish and maintain standards for units designated as senior units to ensure
  that they are accessible and convenient for older persons and persons with
  disabilities.
•  Goal 28: Address the needs of persons experiencing homelessness.
  o  Provide emergency food, shelter and referrals to homeless and very low-income
  individuals and families.
  o  Provide zoning designations for the development of shelters for the homeless.
  o  Cooperate in regional homeless assistance feasibility studies.
  o  Provide referral services and accept referrals from homeless service agencies for
  emergency housing placement.
•  Goal 29: Increase access to safe and adequate housing for people with disabilities.
  o  Ensure access for the disabled in residential, commercial, and public structures.
  o  Educate property managers about the reasonable accommodation provisions of
  the Americans with Disabilities Act and Federal and State fair housing laws through
  the Partners Against Crime program and the fair housing services provider.
•  Goal 30: Implement energy and water conservation measures.
  o  Ensure that energy and water conservation measures are included in all new
  development and redevelopment projects using an energy conservation checklist.
  o  Inform the public about retrofitting their homes with energy and water
  conservation measures.
  o  Incorporate native desert vegetation as a condition of approval for all proposed
  housing projects.
•  Goal 31: Enhance vitality and safety of existing residential neighborhoods.
  o  Actively enforce compliance with health, safety, building, fire, law enforcement and
  other regulations in all neighborhoods.
  o  Actively enforce the City’s property maintenance ordinance.
  o  Improve property maintenance and management by providing training to owners
  and managers.
•  Goal 32: Promote neighborhood versatility by encouraging a mix of new housing
  alternatives to increase affordability and promote home ownership.
  o  Encourage voluntary inclusionary housing by offering incentives to developers.

  City of Palmdale General Plan Update | 26
   Land Use, Community Design and Housing Policy Framework | Spring 2021

o  Evaluate the feasibility of small lots, reduced setbacks or other modifications to
  reduce cost of development.
o  Encourage mixed-use housing in designated areas along transportation corridors
  and other commercial areas.

DATE:  August 17, 2021
TO:  HONORABLE MAYOR AND CITY COUNCIL
FROM:  CITY MANAGER’S OFFICE – FINANCE DIVISION
DISTRICT:  ALL
SUBJECT:  RECEIVE AND FILE THE MONTHLY AND QUARTERLY INVESTMENT
  ACTIVITY REPORTS FOR JUNE 2021.

ISSUE
Receive and file the monthly and quarterly investment activity reports for June 2021.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council accept the monthly and quarterly investment
activity reports for City of Palmdale and Successor Agency for June 2021.

BACKGROUND
Pursuant to Section 16 of the City of Palmdale and Successor Agency Investment
Policy, the City Treasurer shall prepare and present monthly and quarterly reports on
investments to the City Manager/Executive Director and the City Council/Directors.
The reports shall detail the type of investment, name of the issuer, purchase date, date
of maturity, amount of deposit, and rate of interest. This information shall be provided
for all City and Successor Agency pooled investments, as well as for Certificates of
Participation, Revenue Bonds, Tax Allocation Bonds, Assessment Districts and
Community Facilities District accounts which are managed by outside Fiscal Agents.

The monthly and quarterly reports provide a synopsis of the investment activity for the
City of Palmdale and Successor Agency. The reports provide information on assets,
allocations, average maturities, yields, and book valuations.

The interest rates presented are the most current rates available as of the date of this
report.

The market values presented for pooled City and Successor Agency investments are
based on closing prices for the related investment as of the date of this report. This
information was obtained from the Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg Financial Markets,
Capital Market Finances, or other reliable source of market prices.

August 17, 2021

DISCUSSION
Compliance with Investment Policy

For June, the invested portfolio amount for the City of Palmdale totaled $243,863,336
an increase of $55,269,213 from the previous month and $37,878,779 increase in
comparison to last year. The increase in overall portfolio balance from the previous
month is a result of investment purchases and interest received during the current
period. The City purchased six securities in the month of June for a total of
$20,301,367, as well as investment of $20,000,000 into UBS Financial Services
Money Market account and $20,000,000 in LAIF. These purchases were offset by the
maturities of two securities totaling $5,245,000.

The par value of Successor Agency’s portfolio as of June, was $12,806,559. The
balance increased by $1,458,670 from last month due to interest received.

All investments meet criteria appropriate to Section 8 of the Investment Policy. The
portfolios are based on a combination of various investments, including CDs,
Corporate Notes, U.S. Treasury Securities and Government Agency Paper, each
adhering to portfolio percentage limitations.

The Finance Division is the custodian for the City and Successor Agency’s investment
portfolio and follows the three main principles of both entity’s investment policy to 1.)
Investment in financial instruments that mitigate the risk of monetary losses stemming
from market fluctuations, 2.) Establish and maintain a portfolio that has sufficient
liquidity to allow the City and Successor Agency to meet all anticipated cash
requirements, and 3.) Seek out investment instruments that provide a competitive
market rate of return.

Liquidity

One core approach the Finance Division focuses on, is providing liquidity to measure
up to the City and Successor Agency’s operational requirements. Thus, the Finance
Department is currently investing in two pooled funds, LAIF and CAMP. These are
intended for the daily operational activities, used for economic uncertainties and
maintenance needs. The pooled funds provide a higher liquidity ratio to ensure the
City and Successor Agency meet cash flow requirements.

Total LAIF balance for the City of Palmdale is $143,980,704 compared to May’s
balance of $123,980,704. The increase in balance is due to investment of funds to
LAIF.

Successor Agency LAIF balance at the end of June was $5,187,677, a 29.5 percent
decrease from June, but flat to the prior month. The decrease in balance for the year is
due to withdraws to cover monthly expenses and debt service payments.

Diversity

unreasonable and avoidable risks regarding specific security types or individual
financial institutions.

  SOFTWARE-AS-A-SERVICE IN AN AMOUNT NOT TO EXCEED
  $2,205,200

ISSUE
Approve an agreement with Tyler Technologies, Inc. for Software-as-a-Service in an
amount not to exceed $2,205,170.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:

  1. Approve Agreement A-7598 for Software-as-a-Service between the City of
  Palmdale and Tyler Technologies, Inc. not to exceed $2,205,170 for the term of
  seven (7) years commencing August 17, 2021 through August 16, 2028.

  2. Direct the City Attorney to finalize the Agreement and authorize the City Manager
  or his designee to execute the agreement, including making minor and non-
  substantive changes.

DISCUSSION

The Need

The City’s current Electronic Enterprise System, Tyler Technologies, Inc.’s Munis, was
implemented in 2006. The system has served the City Well for fifteen years. However,
there are a few major issues with current Munis that prompted staff to consider
converting to a cloud-based system, known as Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) which will
replace the current system.

The current system provides the functionalities related to financial and HR transactions
with the following operational modules in place:
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Approve Agreement A-7598 Tyler Technologies, Inc.
August 17, 2021

    Accounting/GL
    Contract Management
    Project/Grant Accounting
    Purchase Orders
    Requisitions
    Accounts Receivable
    General Billing
    Munis Office
    Tyler Forms Processing
    CAFR Statement Builder
    Concurrent Users (60)
    HR Management
    Payroll
    Tyler Content Management

Because the current Tyler Munis is a server-based system, staffs have been concerned
about two major risks.

First, concern over operational risk has grown over the past few years, fueled by a
variety of factors. During the Fiscal Year 2019-20 and Fiscal Year 2020-21, staff
experienced significant technical challenges with certain modules as Tyler made newer
versions and patches available to user groups including the City of Palmdale. Although
Tyler will continue to support the server-based Munis and it continues to work in the
ever-changing environment, the enhancements were not functioning as intended for an
extended period. A number of local agencies using server-based Munis have already
switched to SaaS system within the past few years. These are all signals that the server-
based software is slowly being phased out and is closer to the sunset phase of its
product life cycle.

The second major issue with the current Munis system is that there is no site redundancy
in the City’s current infrastructure. Although the city maintains backups, if the primary
hardware that operates the current Munis system fails or otherwise is rendered
inoperable, it cannot be easily replaced and repaired. Additionally, to continue to use
the server-based Munis system the City will need to spend $170,000 in infrastructure
equipment and services in the next five years; $154,000 would be spent in the first year
just to bring the operating environment up-to-date.

Significant risks exist in continued use of current Munis for the critical functions of issuing
payments, receiving revenues, financial reporting, etcetera. The City will invest
thousands of dollars into modernizing server infrastructure only to find out a few years
later that Tyler will phase out the server-based program. In the meantime, the City
continues to operate in an environment that will be marginally improved, unable to take
advantage of modern efficiencies, and ultimately result in a switch of software system.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Approve Agreement A-7598 Tyler Technologies, Inc.
August 17, 2021
Page 3

The goals of switching system now are to eliminate the uncertainty of current Munis life
cycle, improve the system redundancy, and take advantage of technological
efficiencies.

The Solicitation Process

To determine which system would be the best value to the City, staff reviewed the
requests for proposals by other local agencies in California. From this review process,
it was clear that the best solution was to select Munis SaaS by Tyler Technologies, Inc.
Based on the products available for a City of Palmdale’s size, complexity, and price
range, an enterprise solution is limited to a handful of players in the industry; Oracle,
SAP, Peoplesoft, Tyler Technologies, Kronos, Accela, and CentralSquare to name a
few. The solutions from top tier software vendors such as Oracle, SAP, and Peoplesoft
are cost prohibitive while other vendors concentrate on specific Human Capital
Management, Asset Management, Community Development, or Public Works
component.

Staff recommends the City Council to award a contract to Tyler Technologies, Inc. for
the ERP without going through a competitive bidding process based on the City’s Best
Interest per PMC 3.08.080 (C). Tyler has averaged 70 to 90 implementations of Munis
product per year for the past decade. The company has over 4,500 employees, 1,200
of whom support the Munis product. There are approximately 120 clients in California
using the Munis product. The company has had an average annual growth rate of 13
percent since 2002 and carries no debt as a corporation. The company offers a
complete, integrated solution for the City while supporting all federal and State
mandates as part of the City’s support agreement.

Towards the end of the Fiscal Year 2019-20, staff issued a request for proposal for
enhanced timeclock functions, payroll, and HR management. During the Fiscal Year
2020-21, staff short-listed a selected vendors for further evaluations.  The
demonstrations took good part of the fiscal year for each one and included staffs from
all departments. From this process, and after considerable deliberation, it was clear that
the best solution was to select Munis Executime, which will be added to the new Munis
SaaS agreement. Selection of Executime demonstrates Tyler’s comprehensive
solutions that can be easily integrated into the City existing ERP.

I.  Agreement Overview
This SLA operates in conjunction with, and does not supersede or replace any part of, the Agreement. It
outlines the information technology service levels that we will provide to you to ensure the availability of
the application services that you have requested us to provide. All other support services are documented

II.  Definitions. Except as defined below, all defined terms have the meaning set forth in the
Agreement.

Attainment: The percentage of time the Tyler Software is available during a calendar quarter, with
percentages rounded to the nearest whole number.
Client Error Incident: Any service unavailability resulting from your applications, content or equipment, or
the acts or omissions of any of your service users or third-party providers over whom we exercise no
control.
Downtime: Those minutes during which the Tyler Software is not available for your use. Downtime does
not include those instances in which only a Defect is present.
Service Availability: The total number of minutes in a calendar quarter that the Tyler Software is capable
of receiving, processing, and responding to requests, excluding maintenance windows, Client Error
Incidents and Force Majeure.

III.  Service Availability
The Service Availability of the Tyler Software is intended to be 24/7/365. We set Service Availability goals
and measures whether we have met those goals by tracking Attainment.

Whenever you experience Downtime, you must make a support call according to the procedures outlined
in the Support Call Process. You will receive a support incident number.
You must document, in writing, all Downtime that you have experienced during a calendar quarter. You
must deliver such documentation to us within 30 days of a quarter’s end.
The documentation you provide must evidence the Downtime clearly and convincingly. It must include,
for example, the support incident number(s) and the date, time and duration of the Downtime(s).
  b.  Our Responsibilities

with you to identify the cause of the Downtime (including whether it may be the result of a Client Error
Incident or Force Majeure). We will also work with you to resume normal operations.

BACKGROUND
This ADA project will provide a new ADA modular restroom to replace the existing non
accessible restroom at McAdam Park. Approximately 285 feet of sewer line will also be
removed and replaced with a new sewer line that has sufficient slope to address the
maintenance issues of the existing, flat sewer line. An accessible path of travel from the
existing ADA parking to the new restroom will be provided through the replacement of
portions of the existing concrete walkway.

follows:

ISSUE
Adopt Resolution No. CC 2021-071, a Resolution of the City Council of the City of
Palmdale authorizing the Director of Public Works or his designee to utilize Knorr
Systems Inc. as the City’s sole source for aquatics equipment.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council adopt Resolution No. 2021-071 authorizing the
Director of Public Works or his designee to utilize Knorr Systems Inc. as the City’s sole
source for aquatics equipment.

BACKGROUND
Earlier this year a representative of Knorr Systems Inc. approached the Department of
Parks and Recreation with a proposal to provide sole source aquatics equipment and
services for the City of Palmdale.

In the last 15 years, Knorr Systems Inc. has provided all aquatics equipment for McAdam
Park Pool, Drytown Water Park, Oasis Pool, Marie Kerr Pool; and since its opening in
2019, for Courson Pool. The aquatic’s component for each of these projects was
competitively bid for. and in each case Knorr Systems Inc. provided the most competitive
bid to meet the specifications listed in the bid package.

DISCUSSION
Staff from the Parks and Recreation Department, Public Works Department and the City
Attorney’s Office have met to discuss the feasibility of sole sourcing aquatic facilities
equipment and service. Based on criteria found in Palmdale City Competitive Bid
Ordinance 3.08.080 Item B, Knorr Systems Inc. product satisfies the criteria required to
authorize a sole source arrangement.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Adopt Resolution No. CC 2021-071
August 17, 2021
Page 2

Knorr Systems Inc. is well known in the Water Park Industry for proving all in one world
class equipment, service, training, and daily operational support. They provide industry
leading service warranty on their parts & labor. They are local to Southern California and
can provide a timelier service to DryTown Water Park and other aquatic facilities to meet
our needs. From experience, the City has seen other vendors come in at a lower bid
whose quality does not match Knorr Systems, Inc’s quality of product and service.

Use of a single source for aquatics equipment and service also provides a great
advantage in operating and maintaining the system. Maintenance staff has become
thoroughly familiar with Knorr System Inc’s. system, its replacement components, and
regular maintenance schedule. This allows easier stocking of parts, as well as saves
substantially on training and routine maintenance.

The proposed resolution only allows the Public Works Director to sole source, if, in his
opinion, such action is warranted in a particular instance. The Director may, in his
discretion, bid a project and/or secure prices for alternate aquatic systems to ensure
Knorr Systems Inc.’s future bids remain competitive. Staff believes this option will assure
the City continued overall best value in this area.

FISCAL IMPACT
By using Knorr Systems, Inc. as a sole source provider the City will receive direct pricing
without a secondary party mark up. The City of Palmdale and the aquatics facilities will
receive consistent industry leading service, quality parts and labor along with an
approximate 10% annual savings based upon historical bidding results.

  public spaces with exciting programming that promotes active fun for
  everyone.

SUBJECT:  REJECTION OF BID FOR PROJECT NO. 741-A, AVENUE S-8 AND
  40TH STREET EAST WATERLINE IMPROVEMENT PROJECT

ISSUE
Rejection of bid for Project No. 741-A, Avenue S-8 and 40th Street East Waterline
Improvement Project

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Reject bid received for Project No. 741-A, Avenue S-8 and 40th Street East
  Waterline Improvement Project

BACKGROUND
Project No. 741-A will upgrade the existing main water system as a prerequisite for Project
No. 741, Avenue S-8 and 40th Street East Roundabout. Palmdale Water District (PWD)
requires all water mains underneath the new concrete structures to be protected by a
casing. Project No. 741-A includes removal and disposal of existing 12-inch and 16-inch
diameter water mains and all appurtenances, furnish and installation of new 12-inch and
16-inch diameter water mains, steel casing, and water valves, relocation of fire hydrant,
and all other related work. The Engineer’s estimate for this work was approximately
$280,000.

Based on Public Contract Code, in order to have a successful bidder there must be more
than one contractor submitting a bid. The City received only one bid for Project No. 741-
A during the procurement process. Pursuant to Section 20166 and 21321 of the Public
Contract Code, the City of Palmdale has the right to reject all bids and to later rebid the
project.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Rejection of Bids for PN 741-A
August 17, 2021
Page 2

DISCUSSION
One bid was received on July 28, 2021 and is summarized as follows:
Bidder  Location  Amount
1. Cedro Construction  Santa Maria, CA  $436,346

The bid of $436,346 is $156,000 in excess of the engineer’s $280,000 estimate and
contained mathematical errors. Staff recommends that the City Council reject the only bid
received for Project No. 741-A, Avenue S-8 and 40th Street East Waterline Improvement
Project and re-bid the project. Staff believes it would be in the best interest of the City to
reject the bid received and rebid the project.

The project will be re-bid immediately following the rejection of bid and awarded at one of
the September 2021 City Council meetings in efforts to start and complete the work during
Palmdale Water District’s strict water shut off time frame between November 1 and
December 31 of the same year.

FISCAL IMPACT
The total project is funded from S0066, Avenue S-8 and 40th Street East Roundabout
from Measure R and Federal HSIP Grant funds, with a current balance of $4,541,585.

ISSUE
Shall the City Council adopt Resolution No. CC 2021-087 Amending the City’s
Classification and Pay Plan for General Positions?

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council adopt Resolution No. CC 2021-087 Amending
the City’s Classification and Pay Plan for General Positions.

BACKGROUND
The Human Resources Division monitors and evaluates positions within the organization
and makes recommendations based on the needs of the City.

DISCUSSION

The City currently has an Emergency Services Administrator vacancy. This position is
responsible for both the City’s Emergency Services and Safety programs. The City held
two recruitments to fill the position. Both attempts have been unsuccessful. Because
the Emergency Services and Safety fields are separate professions and each require a
different set of skills and knowledge, the City has been unable to find a candidate who is
qualified in both areas.

As a result, staff recommends amending the classification and pay plan and authorizing
a new full-time position of Safety Coordinator at Range 38.

In addition, the California Public Employees’ Retirement System (CalPERS) requires the
City Council to approve Classification and Pay Plans. To comply with CalPERS
guidelines, staff is submitting the Classification and Pay Plan for General Positions for
approval.

  Now, after long accepting their early morning marathons as a given, Palmdale officials are finally talking about
  finding a better way to conduct the public’s business.

  ADVERTISING

  As a result of the May 13 flare-up, Palmdale City Administrator Bob Toone told council members he will present
  them with options for improving the situation at their June 10 meeting. A second regular council meeting each
  month and a council curfew--halting the meetings at a set time such as 11:30 p.m.--are possibilities.

  But council members appear divided on their preferences, and no clear consensus has emerged. Councilman David
  Myers, for instance, favors a second regular meeting each month, but Councilwoman Teri Jones said she opposes it,
  and Councilman Jim Root is skeptical. Ledford, meanwhile, has been pushing his council curfew plan.

  The reasons for the marathon sessions vary. Sometimes a bevy of controversial topics draws a heavy turnout of
  residents eager to talk. Other times council members get caught in drawn-out debates. And oftentimes, part of the
  reason is that the council’s regular agendas, because they have only one a month, include dozens of items.

  Although Palmdale officials are reluctant to shift to twice-a-month meetings, complaining of the extra staff work to
  prepare for the extra sessions, a Times survey of 10 other similarly sized cities in Los Angeles County showed them
  all holding two or more regular council meetings monthly, and almost all saying they finish at earlier hours.

  In the past 17 months, 13 of the 17 regular monthly meetings ended past 11 p.m., seven of those between 1 a.m. and 3
  a.m. and another--the longest, in July 1992--went to 3:18 a.m., city records show. Even after excluding the council’s
  closed-door sessions, which often come last, 12 of the public sessions ended after 11 p.m., according to records.

  Palmdale officials acknowledge they become bleary-eyed and tired as the nights drag on.

  “I can’t defend that as being in the best interest of decision-making,” Ledford said.

  The timing of night council meetings is particularly important in Palmdale, where many residents commute to the
  Los Angeles and San Fernando Valley areas and thus must leave home as early as 4:30 a.m. Palmdale’s regular
  council meetings now are held the second Thursday of each month, meaning the following morning is a workday for
  most.

  At the May 13 Palmdale council meeting, several hundred residents turned out at 7 p.m. to testify on a trio of hot
  items: an increase in trash collection fees, an increase in landscape maintenance fees and a rent-control measure for
  the city’s large number of mobile-home residents.

  Not only were many residents left standing for hours because there is limited seating in the council chambers, but
  many ultimately ended up leaving before the council got to their items because the session went so late.

  “There were a lot of people who wanted to speak but left,” Councilman Root said.

  Ledford acknowledged that how the council handles its scheduling problem probably also will impact residents’
  ability to address their elected officials. While the early morning sessions certainly make it tough on residents, so
  would a plan under discussion by council members to more tightly limit residents’ speaking time to help end the
  meetings earlier.

BACKGROUND
According to The Palmdale Aerospace Academy (“TPAA”) Bylaws, Article 3 Directors,
Section 3.3, the City shall designate three (3) Directors to serve on the Board of
Directors. According to Section 3.3 (b), “All Directors of the Corporation shall serve a

has expired. Ms. Ellen McIsaac has served as a Director on the Board of Directors for

resignation. Pursuant to the Section 3.3 (b), “No Director shall serve more than two (2)
complete, consecutive three-year terms. A Director who has served two (2) such
consecutive three-year terms shall be eligible to serve again as a Director after one (1)
year has passed since the expiration of such Director’s last term of office.” Ms. McIsaac

ISSUE
Approve nomination for reappointment of Commissioner to the Housing Authority.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends pursuant to Palmdale Municipal Code Section 2.080.030 that the City
Council ratify the nomination for reappointment to the Housing Authority as follows:
1. Approve reappointment of the following individual nominated by Mayor Hofbauer to
  serve as Commissioner for a two-year term, set to expire on September 30, 2023.

  1. Christina Fraga-Sanz

BACKGROUND
The purpose of the Housing Authority (“HA”) of the City of Palmdale is to address the
shortage of safe, sanitary housing for persons of low income. The HA is comprised of
seven (7) Commissioners consisting of five (5) City Council members and two (2)
appointed Tenant members. The two (2) appointed tenant members must be tenants in
the Housing Authority properties and at least one (1) of the appointed tenant members
must be age 62 or older. The two (2) appointed tenant members have the same equal
voting rights as the five City Council members. If the tenant member ceases to be a
tenant, he or she shall be disqualified as a member and another tenant shall be
appointed to fill the un-expired term. The tenant member must be a resident in good
standing. Palmdale HA Tenant Members must reside in HA properties as follows:
    Boulders at the Ranch 1
    Boulders at the Ranch 2
    Boulders at the Lake
    La Quinta Apartments
    Summerwood

The term of office is two (2) years. Housing Authority members are not involved in the

of the Ralph M. Brown Act and are required to attend city-sponsored trainings.
The HA meetings are called as needed and are generally held in the City Council
Chamber, located at 38300 Sierra Highway, Suite B, Palmdale, CA on the first Tuesday
of every month at 7:00 p.m. Periodically, additional meetings are held to discuss agenda
items, and open to the public. Approximately a week prior to each meeting, an agenda
packet is sent to each Commissioner to provide the opportunity to prepare for
deliberation of each agenda item.

DISCUSSION
On September 30, 2021, terms of service are set to expire for Commissioners Thomas
Brown and Christina Fraga-Sanz. Commissioner Fraga-Sanz was first appointed to the
HA on December 31, 2018. She has expressed her intent to continue to serve and her
desire for reappointment, as she possesses the institutional knowledge and experience
needed to add continued value. Commissioner Thomas Brown has enjoyed serving the
community. Unfortunately, he is not seeking reappointment and a recruitment for the
vacancy will be open until filled, as the qualified candidate is required to be 62 years
or older.

Pursuant to Resolution No. HA 2020-002 (attached), the Housing Authority authorizes
and approves payment of compensation to the two tenant members appointed as
Commissioners to the Housing Authority of $100.00 for each Housing Authority meeting
attended for a maximum of two meetings per month.

A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF PALMDALR MAKING
CERTAIN FINDINGS, DECLARING THE NEED FOR A HOUSING AUTHORITY TO
FUNCTION IN THE CITY OF P.ALMDALE ANI) DECLARING ITSELF TO BR THE
COMMISSIONERS OF THE HOUSING AUTHORITY

  WHEREAS, Part 2 of Division 24 of the Health and Safety Code
of the State of California, sometimes referred to as the Housing
Authorities Law (Cal. Health and Safety Code Section 34000 et
  g.J, provides in part that in each city there is a public body
corporate and politic known as the housing authority of the city,
and that the housing authority shall not transact any business or
exercise its powers unless, by resolution, the governing body of
the city declares that there is need for a housing authority to
function in it.
  WHEREAS,  the Housing Authorities Law provides that the
governing body of a city may make the determination upon its own
motion.
  WHEREAS, the Housing Authorities Law further provides that the
governing body of a city may adopt the resolution if it finds
either of the following: (a) insanitary or unsafe inhabited
dwellings exist; or (b) that there is a shortage of safe or
sanitary dwelling accommodations in the city available to persons
of low income at rentals they can afford.

  WHEREAS, the Housing Authorities Law further provides that the
governing body at the time of adoption of the resolution or at any
time thereafter may declare itself to be the commissioners of the
housing authority.
  WHEREAS, mobile homes constitute an important housing resource
in the City of Palmdale.
  WHEREAS, Mobile home owners are often persons of low or
moderate income, including seniors and families with children, who
are required  pay a disproportionate amount of their income on
housing costs,  ncludng space rent in mobile home parks.
  WHEREAS, there 15 a shortage of safe or sanitary dwelling
accommodations 1r the City of Palmdale available to persons of low
income at rentals they can afford, specifically including a
shortage of well-managed mobile home parks in the City of Palmdale
with respect to which long-term affordability for low income
persons  s ensured as the result of recorded agreements or
covenants.

  -1-
   WHEREAS, to address the shortage of well-managed mobile home
parks in the City of Palmdale with respect to which long-term
affordability for low income persons is ensured as the result of
recorded agreements or covenants, there is a need for a housing
authority to function in the City of Palmdale.

  NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED by the City Council of the City
of Palmdale as follows:
  Section 1.  The City Council of the City of Palmdale hereby
finds and declares that the above recitals are true and correct.
  Section 2.  The City Council of the City of Palmdale hereby
finds that there is a shortage of safe or sanitary dwelling
accommodations in the City of Palmdale available to persons of low
income at rentals they can afford, specifically including a
shortage of well-managed mobile home parks in the City of Palmdale
with respect to which long-term affordability for low income
persons is ensured by recorded agreements or covenants.
  Section 3.  The City Council of the City of Palmdale hereby
declares that there is need for a housing authority to function in
the City of Palmdale.

  Section 4.  The City Council of the City of Palmdale hereby
declares itself to be the commissioners of the housing authority,
and shall be vested with all of the rights, powers, duties, and
privileges and immunities vested in an authority by the Housing
Authorities Law.
  Section 5.  The City Manager of the City of Palmdale shall
serve as the Executive Director of the housing authority, with full
authority to execute documents and enter into contracts on behalf
of the housing authority.  The City Clerk shall serve as the
Secretary of the housing authority.  The staff of the City of
Palmdale shall furnish to the housing authority such necessary
staff services associated with or required by the housing authority
and which could be performed by the staff of an authority.
  Section 6. This Resolution shall take effect immediately upon
its adoption.

ISSUE
Adopt Resolution No. CC 2021-070, a Resolution of the City Council of the City Council
of the City of Palmdale declaring its intention to establish the Palmdale Tourism
Improvement District (PTID).

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Adopt Resolution No. CC 2021-070, a Resolution of the City Council of the City of
  Palmdale declaring its intention to establish the PTID.
  2. Authorize the City Manager or their designee to execute any documents related to
  the establishment of the PTID.

BACKGROUND
In California, Tourism Improvement Districts (TID) are primarily formed pursuant to the
Property and Business Improvement District Law of 1994 (94 Law). This law allows for
the creation of special benefit assessment districts to raise funds within a specific
geographic area. The key difference between TIDs and other special benefit assessment
districts is that funds raised are returned to the private non-profit corporation governing
the TID.

TID benefits:
   They are customized to fit the needs of each destination;
   They allow for a wide range of services, including destination marketing, tourism
  promotion, and sales lead generation;
   They are designed, created and governed by those who will pay the assessment;
   They provide a stable funding source for tourism promotion; and,
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Proposed Resolution No. CC 2021-070
August 17, 2021
Page 2

    Funds cannot be diverted for other government programs.

Over the past twelve months, City staff has met with the hotels in Palmdale to establish
a proposed PTID. Hotels in Palmdale have lower occupancy and overnight stays during
holidays and weekends, the proposed PTID attempts to increase overnight stays through
enhancements in city amenities and tourism opportunities.

The proposed PTID would be a partnership between the City and the hotels in Palmdale
to create additional tourism and visitor opportunities that both visitors and residents could
enjoy. The benefits a TID can provide come in a variety of forms such as signature events,
enhancing the current tourism attractions, development of additional destinations and
infrastructure improvements. This increase in tourism and business travel would positively
impact hotels, restaurants, and entertainment businesses.

TIDs are self-assessment districts, which means that lodging business owners within the
PTID fund the TID, and those funds are used to provide services that are desired by and
benefit those lodging businesses within the PTID. TIDs utilize the efficiencies of private
sector operation in the market-based promotion of tourism. These special assessment
districts allow lodging business owners to organize their efforts to increase tourism.

DISCUSSION
The hotel owners and managers throughout Palmdale are proposing to form the PTID
for a five-year term. The proposed services include special events, infrastructure
improvements and enhancing current visitor attractions. All services provided by the
PTID are intended to attract new visitors.

Hotel business owners decided to pursue formation of a PTID to create a revenue source
devoted to marketing Palmdale as a tourist meeting and event destination. If established,
the PTID would generate approximately $900,000 annually for promotion of travel and
tourism specific to Palmdale.

The Management District Plan (Attachment 2) includes the proposed boundary of the
proposed PTID, a service plan and budget, and governance. The PTID will include all
current and future lodging businesses within the boundaries of Palmdale.

As proposed, the PTID is expected to have a five-year term, beginning November 1, 2021
through October 31, 2026. The self-assessment will be implemented beginning
November 1, 2021. Once per year, beginning on the anniversary of the TID formation,
there is a 30-day period in which business owners paying 50% or more of the total self-
assessment may protest and begin proceedings to terminate the TID.

The annual self-assessment rate is two percent of gross short-term room rental revenue.
Based on the benefit received, assessments will not be collected on stays of more than

The City will collect the self-assessment from each lodging business located within the
PTID boundaries and distribute the assessment to the PTID, which will have the
responsibility of managing TID programs as provided in this Management District Plan.
The PTID shall pay the City a fee equal to one percent of the amount of assessment
collected to cover the costs of collection and administration.

  I.  OVERVIEW
Developed by local hoteliers and the City of Palmdale (City), the Palmdale Tourism Improvement
District (PTID) is an assessment district proposed to provide specific benefits to payors, by funding
marketing and sales promotion efforts for assessed businesses. This approach has been used
successfully in other destination areas throughout the country to provide the benefit of additional
room night sales directly to payors.

Location:  The PTID includes all lodging businesses, existing and in the future, available for
  public occupancy located within the boundaries of the City of Palmdale, as shown on
  the map in Section III.

Services:  The PTID is designed to provide specific benefits directly to payors by increasing
  awareness and demand for room night sales. Sales, marketing & communications and
  destination development programs will increase demand for overnight tourism and
  market payors as tourist, meeting and event destinations, thereby increasing demand
  for room night sales.

Budget:  The total PTID annual assessment budget for the initial year of its five (5) year
  operation is anticipated to be approximately $900,000. A similar budget is expected to
  apply to subsequent years, but this budget is expected to fluctuate as room sales do.

Cost:  The annual assessment rate is two percent (2%) of gross short-term room rental
  revenue. Based on the benefit received, assessments will not be collected on: stays of
  more than thirty (30) consecutive days; stays of any officer or employee of a foreign
  government who is exempt by reason of express provision of federal law or
  international treaty; and stays pursuant to contracts executed prior to November 1,
  2021.

Collection:  The City shall be responsible for collecting the assessment on a monthly basis
  (including any delinquencies, penalties and interest) from each lodging business
  located in the boundaries of the PTID. The City shall take all reasonable efforts to
  collect the assessments from each lodging business.

Duration:  The PTID will have a five (5) year life, beginning November 1, 2021 through October
  31, 2026. Once per year, beginning on the anniversary of PTID formation, there is a
  thirty (30) day period in which owners paying fifty percent (50%) or more of the
  assessment may protest and initiate a City Council hearing on PTID termination.

Management: Visit Palmdale (VP) will serve as the PTID’s Owners’ Association. The Owners’
  Association is charged with managing funds and implementing programs in
  accordance with this Plan, and must provide annual reports to the City Council.

  C. California Constitutional Compliance
The PTID assessment is not a property-based assessment subject to the requirements of Proposition
218. Courts have found Proposition 218 limited the term ‘assessments’ to levies on real property.1
Rather, the PTID assessment is a business-based assessment, and is subject to Proposition 26.
Pursuant to Proposition 26 all levies are a tax unless they fit one of seven exceptions. Two of these
exceptions apply to the PTID, a “specific benefit” and a “specific government service.” Both require
that the costs of benefits or services do not exceed the reasonable costs to the City of conferring the
benefits or providing the services.

  1. Specific Benefit
Proposition 26 requires that assessment funds be expended on, “a specific benefit conferred or
privilege granted directly to the payor that is not provided to those not charged, and which does not
exceed the reasonable costs to the local government of conferring the benefit or granting the
privilege.”2 The services in this Plan are designed to provide targeted benefits directly to assessed
